title: Interaction Scaling: Grounding the Third Axis of Test-Time Compute
hook: Reasoning longer and sampling more both mine the same frozen weights — they can't tell a model anything new. Let it poke a real tool instead, and a coding loop hits 100% pass rate with zero variance.
key_points: Reasoning-longer and sample-more are both internal — every extra token comes from the same frozen weights, so neither teaches the model anything new.
Interaction is a third axis: propose an artifact, let a real instrument observe it, then revise — each cycle imports a genuinely new observation.
On hard coding tasks, a grounded proposer-reviewer loop hits 100% pass rate with zero variance, while reasoning-only and oracle best-of-N both plateau below it.
On visual artifacts, a VLM judge rates 14 of 15 broken figures 'perfect' — fooled by the screenshot; a real layout-measuring tool removes 40-74% of defects.
The gain only appears when both the feedback and the scoring metric come from an instrument that actually observes the real flaw.
content_html: There are two familiar ways to spend more compute at inference time: let the model think longer, or sample many attempts and keep the best. This paper points out both are dead ends in the same way — every extra token still comes from the same frozen weights and the same prompt, so neither can hand the model a fact it doesn't already possess.
extra_html: The authors study a third axis: interaction. A model proposes an artifact, an external instrument observes how it actually behaves, and the model revises based on that real observation — each cycle imports genuinely new information rather than re-mining what's already inside the weights. They argue a single variable, grounding, governs whether this works: the feedback driving revision and the metric scoring the result both have to come from an instrument that truly observes the flaw. On hard coding tasks at a fixed token budget, reasoning-only and best-of-N sampling both plateau (best-of-N even with an oracle picking the winning sample), while a proposer-reviewer loop that actually runs the code keeps improving, reaching a perfect 100% pass rate with no variance across runs — and the effect holds across three model families. The starker demonstration is visual: ask a vision-language model to judge screenshots of rendered layouts, and it calls 14 of 15 visibly broken figures "perfect," fooled by what the screenshot conceals. Swap in a tool that measures the actual layout geometry, and the same revision loop removes 40-74% of real defects across four different modalities. Bojie Li and Noah Shi, arXiv 2026.

related.title: LLM-as-a-Verifier: Verification as a New Scaling Axis
related.hook: Everyone scales pretraining, post-training, and test-time compute. This paper argues verification — checking if a solution is correct — is its own scaling axis, and hits SOTA on four agentic benchmarks.

related.title: When More Sampling Hurts: The Modal Ceiling and Correlation Ceiling of Test-Time Scaling
related.hook: Sample a reasoning model dozens of times and coverage keeps climbing — but picking the right answer from the pile plateaus fast, and extra samples past that point can backfire.

flashcards.prompt: Why do the two standard test-time compute axes (reasoning longer, sampling more) share a hidden ceiling?
flashcards.back_html: Both are internal — every extra token still comes from the same frozen weights and prompt, so neither can give the model information it doesn't already have.

flashcards.prompt: On hard coding tasks at a fixed token budget, what did the grounded proposer-reviewer loop achieve that reasoning-only and best-of-N sampling could not?

choices.text: 100% pass rate with zero run-to-run variance, while the others plateaued below it
Slightly better accuracy, but with much higher variance
The same accuracy, just using less compute
Worse accuracy but faster wall-clock time

flashcards.explanation_html: Best-of-N plateaued even with an oracle selecting the best sample; only the grounded interaction loop kept improving, hitting a perfect, zero-variance result.

flashcards.prompt: Why did a VLM-as-judge rate 14 of 15 visibly broken figures as 'perfect,' while a layout-measuring tool caught the same defects?
flashcards.back_html: The screenshot the VLM looked at hid the flaws from view; a tool that measures actual layout geometry observes the real defect directly, removing 40-74% of them across four modalities.
